# Katarina Schneider

Oulu, Finland | katarina.schneider@mail.example

## Education

**MSc Applied Physics**, Merihaka University, 2000

## Work Experience

**Signal Processing Engineer** | Nordkom Radar Systems, Oulu
2001 – present

- Designed and implemented adaptive beamforming algorithms for Nordkom’s L-band ground-penetrating radar products, including a 16-element phased-array receiver chain that reached production in 2014.
- Wrote and maintained the real-time signal conditioning module in C++ for the RX-4100 radar front end, running on a Xilinx Zynq SoC with a 2 ms frame-processing deadline.
- Responsible for RF characterisation campaigns in Nordkom’s anechoic chamber: antenna pattern measurements and receiver-chain calibration using Keysight PNA-X network analysers and Rohde & Schwarz spectrum analysers.
- All internal communication and documentation in English since 2003, when Nordkom adopted it company-wide following the merger with a Danish subsidiary.
- Based in Oulu since joining in 2001; relocated from Helsinki after completing MSc.

## Projects

**Subsurface Imaging Reconstruction Pipeline** (2018–2020)
Applied inverse-scattering methods from wave physics — building directly on my applied-physics thesis work at Helsinki — to develop a 3D volumetric reconstruction pipeline for Nordkom’s GPR data. The pipeline processes raw multi-channel array data into subsurface images used by civil-engineering and utility-mapping clients. In production since 2020.

## Skills

- **Python (production):** Designed, built, and maintain Nordkom’s automated calibration and regression-test pipeline (~12k lines, pytest, Jenkins CI); in daily use across the engineering group since 2017.
- MATLAB
- C, C++ (embedded real-time targets)
- Signal processing: spectral analysis, array processing, image reconstruction
- Test equipment: network analysers, spectrum analysers, signal generators, oscilloscopes
application.cover_letter_markdown:
After twenty-five years at Nordkom Radar Systems here in Oulu, I have what amounts to a very specific kind of expertise: taking array signal processing from concept through to embedded hardware that works reliably in the field. The work has changed substantially since I joined in 2001 — from hand-tuning analogue receiver chains and debugging with oscilloscopes to software-defined array architectures and automated Python-driven test pipelines — but at the core it has always been about making real-time signal processing run correctly on real hardware under real constraints.

What draws me to the Senior Signal Processing Engineer position at Kaikuvaara is the domain. Your instrument electronics push the same fundamentals I have been applying for years — array processing, embedded DSP, calibration, RF front-end characterisation — but in contexts where the constraints are tighter and the margin for error is smaller than anything I encounter in ground-penetrating radar. I have spent most of my career on adaptive beamforming algorithms, fitting DSP code within hard timing budgets on embedded targets, and building calibration procedures robust enough to survive harsh deployment conditions. These skills transfer. What changes is the application context, and Kaikuvaara’s is the one I want.

At Nordkom I own complete signal chains from antenna through to processed output. That has meant understanding the full path — not just the algorithm, but how it behaves when the ADC clips, when temperature drift shifts the RF response, when the embedded platform throttles under load. The ground-penetrating radar work has been a thorough teacher because the conditions are harsh and the customers care about reliability more than novelty. I think that mentality maps well to what you build.

In your description the emphasis on both embedded signal processing and broader system-level work stands out to me. At Nordkom I have always done both — algorithm design, the C++ implementation on the target hardware, the Python test infrastructure around it — and the RF characterisation work besides. Engineers who sit comfortably across that whole range are not common, and it is what I would bring.

The practical side is simple. I live in Oulu, I know the local engineering community, and English has been my primary working language for over twenty years — since Nordkom’s 2003 merger, all my design reviews, reports, and client communication have been in English. I am not looking for a lifestyle change. I am looking for harder problems.

Nordkom has been a good place to build depth, and I am not leaving because anything is wrong. After this many years, though, the product cycle repeats: different hardware generations, different customers, same class of problem. I would rather take my toolkit somewhere it keeps growing.

My CV is attached.

Katarina Schneider

The Senior Signal Processing Engineer role in Oulu is directly relevant to the work I have been doing at Kajanti Avionics since January 2024. I want to lay out what I bring and where I see the fit, keeping in mind that my experience is shorter than what a senior title usually implies.

My most relevant project at Kajanti has been a phased-array receiver prototype for a wideband digital monitoring system. I was responsible for the beamforming stage of the processing pipeline — implementing a frequency-domain adaptive beamformer that steers nulls toward known interference sources. The array was a 12-element linear configuration, and my work covered the spatial filtering from raw ADC samples through to interference-suppressed output channels. The project ran from late 2024 through mid-2025 and confirmed that array signal processing is the direction I want to build my career in.

Before joining Kajanti I completed my MSc at Bukak National University in 2023. The programme was in a different field from what Kaikuvaara works in, but since graduating I have been deliberately building signal processing depth in an industrial setting. I chose Kajanti because it put me close to real signal processing problems rather than keeping me on a purely academic analysis track.

The practical side is straightforward. I am a Finnish citizen and have been based in Oulu since starting at Kajanti. Language, location, and logistics are not issues.

What I can offer concretely: two and a half years of hands-on digital signal processing work at Kajanti, the phased-array beamforming project I described, and a steep learning curve that I have no intention of flattening. I am aware this is a senior-level role and that my career is shorter than what most applicants will bring. I believe the technical direction is right, though, and that the breadth I am still building is something I would develop faster at a company like Kaikuvaara than anywhere else.

I would welcome the chance to discuss my work in more detail.

Matti Heikkinen

Signal Processing Engineer

## Skills & Tools

- **Python (production):** Own and maintain Boreal’s internal calibration data pipeline — approx. 15k lines, fully unit-tested (pytest), CI/CD via GitLab, used daily by the 20-person engineering team.
- C (embedded real-time), MATLAB, Simulink
- Signal processing: array processing, spectral analysis, demodulation
- RF test equipment: VNA, spectrum analyser, signal generator

---

## Experience

**Signal Processing Engineer** — Boreal Photonics
2016 – present

- Maintained and extended Boreal’s production calibration pipeline in Python, moving it from ad-hoc scripts to a tested, CI-integrated codebase over 2017–2019.
- Conducted regular RF characterisation of photodetector front-end electronics using Rohde & Schwarz ZVL vector network analysers and Keysight N9020A spectrum analysers; responsible for gain flatness and noise-figure verification on incoming sensor modules.
- Since 2022, leading a four-person signal processing subteam responsible for Boreal’s next-generation sensor readout architecture. Hiring, sprint planning, code review, and technical direction.
- All work conducted in English (Boreal’s working language); quarterly progress presentations to international customers including two Japanese optics firms and a German automotive tier-1.

---

## Projects

**Optical Phased-Array Beam Steering Module** (2020–2021)
Designed and implemented digital beamforming algorithms for Boreal’s 64-element silicon-photonic beam steering prototype. Implemented a modified Capon beamformer optimised for the array’s irregular element geometry, with real-time null placement for co-channel interference suppression.

**Embedded Sensor Readout Firmware** (2019)
Wrote the real-time DSP firmware in C for Boreal’s photodetector readout evaluation board (ARM Cortex-M4 target). Sixteen-channel synchronous demodulation with a 50-microsecond loop budget, deployed on production evaluation units shipped to customers.

**Publication**
V. Jarvinen et al., “Adaptive interference suppression in irregular optical phased arrays,” SESE Transactions on Signal Processing, vol. 70, 2022.

**Multi-Sensor Integration Campaign** (2023, Oulu)
Coordinated a three-month sensor integration and field-test campaign at Boreal’s Oulu facility. Relocated from the Helsinki office for the project; remained at the Oulu site and have been based there since.

---

## Education

**MSc Materials Science and Engineering** — Yangtze Delta Institute of Technology, 2015
application.cover_letter_markdown:
When I started at Boreal Photonics in 2016, I had an MSc in Materials Science from Yangtze Delta Institute of Technology and no formal signal processing training. What drew me into the field was the sensor characterisation work during my thesis — the signal processing chain turned out to be more interesting to me than the material itself. Boreal was looking for someone to help with sensor readout electronics and was willing to let me learn the signal processing side on the job.

Ten years later, the gap between what my degree says and what I actually do has become the defining feature of my career. I have published on array processing in SESE Transactions on Signal Processing. I write production embedded firmware and production Python code that runs in deployed systems. I do regular RF characterisation using vector network analysers and spectrum analysers. I have been leading a four-person signal processing subteam since 2022. None of that was in my MSc curriculum — I built it by doing the work, reading what I needed, and solving problems that required me to learn the underlying theory properly. I believe that demonstrated competence is at least as valid as a degree in the right field, and I think my track record makes the case clearly.

The Senior Signal Processing Engineer role at Kaikuvaara is a natural next step for me. I have been based in Oulu since relocating for a project in 2023 and want to stay. The instrument work Kaikuvaara does pushes into domains that interest me, and I want to be somewhere the signal processing challenges are the core product rather than a supporting function.

I know my academic background is not what your posting asks for. Most applicants will have studied electrical engineering or physics. What I offer instead is a decade of real engineering work that got me to the same place by a different path, and a record — publication, production code, team responsibility — that I think speaks plainly enough for an interview to confirm.

My CV has the specifics.

Ville Jarvinen

What keeps me coming back to Kaikuvaara’s listing is the nature of the work itself. I have been following the remote-sensing instrument space from the edges of my own career at Aurinko Avionics for most of the past eight years, reading the published literature on SAR payload signal processing and scatterometer electronics and thinking about how what I do daily connects to that world. The chance to work at a company where spaceborne and airborne instrument development is the core business, not a tangential product line, is what motivated this application. I did not send this broadly — I applied because Kaikuvaara is the specific company I want to work for.

At Aurinko, my work has been in signal processing for communications subsystems — modulation and demodulation chain design, signal integrity analysis, wideband spectral characterisation. Related to what Kaikuvaara does but not identical. There is one project, however, that connects directly, and I want to describe it because it was the work that confirmed my direction.

In 2022 I was part of a team developing a phased-array antenna verification system for Aurinko’s next-generation communication module. My contribution was the beamforming calibration pipeline: I designed the amplitude and phase correction algorithms that compensated for element-to-element manufacturing variation across a 32-element rectangular array, and validated the resulting beam patterns against analytical predictions. The project ran for about eight months. By the end we had a calibrated array producing patterns within 0.5 dB of the target sidelobe levels. That work is the closest I have come to what I understand Kaikuvaara’s core signal processing to involve, and it was the most technically satisfying project of my career so far.

I also have experience with satellite and airborne platform systems, which I know are central to your instrument portfolio.

My electrical engineering degree from KUT gave me the fundamentals — Fourier analysis, linear systems, digital communications theory — and my time at Aurinko has filled in the practical side. I am a Finnish citizen, I have worked in English throughout my career, and I understand that mission-critical instrument work demands discipline in both the engineering and the engineer.

What I do not have is deep experience in remote-sensing instrument electronics specifically. My signal processing at Aurinko has been in the communications subsystem space rather than in imaging or observation payloads. But the underlying signal processing is closely related, and I believe the transition is achievable — especially given how much comes down to the same array processing and DSP fundamentals.

I would genuinely welcome the chance to discuss this with your team. This is not a speculative application. Kaikuvaara is the company I have been hoping would post a signal processing role, and I wanted to make the strongest possible case for the interview.

Marko Korhonen

application.cover_letter_markdown:
Two things converged to make me apply for this role. The first is that Kaikuvaara builds the kind of instruments I find most interesting — remote-sensing payloads where the signal processing is the entire point, not a peripheral function. The second is personal: my partner grew up in Oulu and we have been planning to move there for some time. When I saw the Senior Signal Processing Engineer posting, the overlap was too clear not to act on.

I should be upfront about where I am in my career. I graduated from Kallavesi in 2022 with an MSc in Applied Physics and have been at Polaris RF Labs in Espoo since mid-2023. That is three years of professional experience, not the tenure a senior title usually implies. I am applying anyway because the trajectory matters more to me than the calendar, and I think the work I have done at Polaris and the problems I want to solve align well with what Kaikuvaara needs.

At Polaris my focus has been on signal analysis and sensor characterisation — developing the algorithms and tooling that help the engineering team understand what their sensors are actually doing. My main deliverable has been a production Python pipeline that processes around fifty gigabytes of raw sensor data per day, performs automated quality scoring, and feeds the results into the team’s dashboard. It was a proper software engineering project — tested, logged, CI/CD, used by a dozen people — not a notebook someone would throw away.

What draws me to Kaikuvaara specifically is the mission-critical side. Instruments operating on spaceborne or airborne platforms have to be right the first time, and the signal processing behind them has to account for every noise source, every calibration drift, every edge case that a benign lab environment would never surface. That kind of constraint is what makes engineering interesting to me. The industrial sensing problems I work on at Polaris are useful but forgiving — if something drifts, you recalibrate and move on. With remote-sensing instruments on a platform you cannot physically reach after deployment, the bar is fundamentally higher. I want to work to that bar.

I am a Czech-Finnish dual citizen, so work authorisation is not a concern. The move to Oulu is already in motion for family reasons, and if it happens to coincide with a role at Kaikuvaara, that would be the best possible outcome. I have contributed to projects involving satellite systems and have some experience coordinating technical work across small teams, though my depth in both areas is still developing.

The honest summary: I bring a strong physics foundation, real production software skills, and a specific interest in the kind of work you do — but less experience than you probably want. I am betting that an interview would show enough substance to justify giving a motivated physicist with genuine engineering output a chance to grow into the title.

Erik Novak

application.cover_letter_markdown:
Tuulenkaari Satellite Systems has been my employer for close to nineteen years now, and I think that says something about the kind of engineer I am: I prefer depth over breadth, I like working on things that take a long time to get right, and I am not easily restless. But I am writing this letter because the work at Kaikuvaara looks like the right reason to make a change.

My role at Tuulenkaari has been consistent. I process and verify signal data, I maintain the workflows that turn raw inputs into deliverables, and I keep the quality pipeline running. It is detailed, steady work that demands precision and a tolerance for the unglamorous parts of engineering. I took a year off in 2009–2010 to travel, came back, and have been at it since. The company moved from Tampere to Oulu in 2012 and I moved with it.

What I would bring to Kaikuvaara is operational reliability. I know what it takes to keep a data processing chain running for years without the kind of errors that compound downstream. I am good at documentation — I personally converted Tuulenkaari’s entire technical documentation archive from Finnish to English when the company changed its working language, more than 340 documents, and I know the difference between documentation that exists on paper and documentation that actually helps the next person. And I have been working in Oulu long enough to know the engineering community and the practical realities of building a career here.

I recognise that this role asks for things I cannot claim. My career has been narrower than what a senior signal processing position at Kaikuvaara probably requires, and I have spent most of it in one company doing one kind of work. I do not have the range of someone who has moved between companies and application domains. What I do have is almost two decades of disciplined, detail-oriented signal processing operations, and I think there is a place for that kind of reliability at a company where precision is non-negotiable.

I am a Danish citizen and have lived in Finland since 2004. I have been based in Oulu since 2012 and I am not planning to leave. English has been my working language at Tuulenkaari since 2018 and was my daily language at university before that.

I would be glad to discuss what I can bring in more practical detail.

Nadia Jensen

- Optical signal processing algorithm development and sensor data pipeline architecture, applying the wave physics and mathematical modelling foundations from my RRIT Physics degree to spectral calibration, detector characterisation, and noise analysis.
- Designing and maintaining MATLAB-based simulation and analysis tooling for Sinikaari’s sensor product line.

Career break (2009 – 2010)
Took a year for further study, completing a postgraduate certificate in data science at Riddarfjarden University.

## Key Projects

Kantele Cross-Border Optical Sensing Collaboration (2019–2021)
Participated in a Kantele-funded research collaboration with university and industry partners in Norway and Denmark. Nigerian-Swedish dual national with full EU work rights; handled the Swedish-side formal reporting to the funding body.

Sinikaari Sensor Characterisation Handbook (2022)
Authored a 120-page internal reference handbook on optical sensor characterisation methods for Sinikaari’s engineering team. Written entirely in English as part of the company’s transition to English as its working language.

## Skills

- MATLAB, Simulink, LabVIEW
- Signal processing: spectral analysis, noise characterisation, optical sensor modelling

application.cover_letter_markdown:
At this point in my career what I want is a role where the physics matters as much as the engineering. I have been at Sinikaari Optics for seventeen years — with a one-year break in 2009–2010 — working on optical signal processing, and the work has been good. But Sinikaari is a product company, and over time the physics has been pushed further into the background while the product engineering has taken over. The sensor characterisation and spectral calibration work that used to be the centre of my job have become maintenance tasks, and the interesting problems have been solved.

Kaikuvaara’s Senior Signal Processing Engineer role looks like the kind of position where the physics is still live. The instrument electronics for remote-sensing payloads demand a deep understanding of the physical processes behind the signals, not just the processing techniques applied to them. That is what I trained for at RRIT and what I have spent seventeen years building on at Sinikaari, and I would like to do it somewhere it is still the main challenge.

What I bring concretely: a strong physics background (MSc from RRIT) that I have applied continuously in industry for close to two decades, a record of careful sensor characterisation and calibration work, and experience writing technical documentation in English that other engineers actually use. I wrote Sinikaari’s 120-page sensor characterisation reference handbook, which has been the team’s primary working document since 2022 — I mention it because documentation quality is something I care about and something I know not every candidate will.

The career break in 2009–2010 was for a postgraduate data science certificate at Riddarfjarden University. It broadened my quantitative toolkit, but it also confirmed that my interest is in physics-based signal processing, not in data engineering as a field.

I am a Swedish and Nigerian dual citizen with full EU work rights, so there are no authorisation issues. I am planning a move to Oulu — my partner has accepted a position there — and the timing coincides with this opening, which is part of why I am applying now.

I have published at conferences in the optical sensing space, though my record is modest rather than extensive.

I would be happy to go through my work at Sinikaari in more detail.

Farid Okafor
